entries.title: Depth of field and motion blur are regular effects
entries.summary: Depth of field and motion blur are no longer experimental: add the effect to a camera profile and it works on Metal, OpenGL and Vulkan.
body: Both effects used to need an environment variable. Now `depthOfField` and `motionBlur` in a project's `postfx` or a camera profile work right away, like bloom or colour grading. They default to the High quality tier, motion blur needs an HDR frame. `AIVERSE_PRISMA_DOF=0` and `AIVERSE_PRISMA_MOTION_BLUR=0` remain to turn them off.

Depth of field works from hardware depth or from distance in metres along the camera (`metricFocus`); LENS sets the focus from lens parameters. Motion blur follows camera motion and the velocity of moving objects.
entries.verified: The same HDR scene on Metal and OpenGL (Mac) and on Vulkan (Android, Adreno 610): focused on the scene the frame stays sharp, focused near the camera it blurs clearly; a turning camera with motion blur smears the frame, a still one is left alone. PRISMA's report marks each effect as drawn.
entries.limits: An approximation, not a physical lens model: no hexagonal bokeh or depth layer separation. On weak mobile GPUs both stay off by default below the High tier.

entries.author: prisma

entries.title: LUMA on Vulkan and Android: direct light, dynamic GI and camera-following cascades
entries.summary: Luma and dynamic GI now run on Vulkan and are checked on an Android phone, and GI cascades follow the camera through large worlds.
body: Luma — direct lighting for thousands of point and spot lights with geometry shadows, GGX reflections and temporal denoising — used to run on Metal only. The same computation now runs on Vulkan, so Luma runs on Android, and on Windows and Linux when Vulkan is selected.

Dynamic GI has a `"scroll": true` mode: up to three probe cascades follow the camera in whole cells. Probes that stay keep their light, cells entering the volume are cleared and traced again — stale light from another place is never shown. The geometry around the camera is loaded as it moves. GI stays on screen while probes update.
TerraWeave terrain tiles feed dynamic GI as soon as they are built.
entries.verified: Samsung Galaxy A05s phone (Adreno 610, Vulkan): Luma in 9 scenes (diffuse, metal, PBR, spot lights, shadows) and dynamic GI on CPU and GPU, with three cascades and with the camera moving away and back, match the CPU reference. The same scenes are checked on Metal.
entries.limits: On Android these are test scenes, not a game: performance on weak phones has not been measured. CPU GI cascades do not scroll.

entries.title: Digital humans: soft facial shadows with adaptive resolution
entries.summary: Shadow map resolution follows the character's size on screen, and the studio light gives a soft portrait shadow — no steps on the neck or ragged edge by the nose.
body: A shared CPU AdaptiveShadowResolution policy picks a 1024, 2048 or 4096 shadow map from viewport height, camera distance and field of view and the share of the frame the character covers. It upgrades at 15% excess demand and downgrades only after 60 frames of low demand, so the resolution does not jump.
The VIVID portrait key light uses soft PCF instead of the general PCSS: an artistic facial filter, not a physically exact area light. Gameplay lighting and shaders are unchanged.
entries.verified: CTest adaptive_shadow_resolution: 1/1 PASS in Release with assertions; native VIVID Creator and Studio builds; video of 168 frames at 1500×920, 24 fps, 0 pipeline failures. Frames are native output without retouching.
entries.limits: The density estimate is conservative, not per pixel; these are not cascaded or virtual shadow maps. Lower resolution tiers at full body are not confirmed with this asset.

entries.author: vivid

entries.title: TERRA ground without tiling or blotches
entries.summary: Up close the ground samples grass, sand and rock from shared world-space detail layers instead of the baked tile texture; a second rotated lookup and macro noise break the repeat.
body: Previously a 64 m tile was baked into a 1024 px texture (about 6 cm per pixel) with top-down grass, which stretched into blotches on slopes. Now the tile texture only stores layer weights (bilinear) and the 4 m detail layers use dominant-axis projection, so slopes do not stretch.

Against tiling, grass and sand get a second lookup rotated ~53° and rescaled, mixed by world gradient noise, plus a two-octave brightness variation (23 m and 7 m). The graph stays within 16 samples; material graphs gain a nodeBudget of up to 192 nodes.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: close-up bank frames; shader_graph test (nodeBudget).
entries.limits: Enabled on the review copy; the main AlpineValley project still uses baked textures.

entries.title: TerraWeave forest: a whole tree per draw, impostors in the distance
entries.summary: Identical trees now render as one instanced draw per detail level instead of one draw per branch, and distant trees use impostors baked from the near model.
body: With hierarchical wind a tree becomes one model with three tiers (full, reduced, minimal); FloraView picks the tier and Renderer3D instances identical trees per primitive. A forest frame went from ~6000 draws to 110–177.
The impostor atlas is baked by rasterising the near model with 2×2 supersampling and colour bleeding, so a distant tree keeps its silhouette and crown colour.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), editor: same-scene draw call and GPU time measurements before/after; tests wind_rig, terraweave_model, terraweave_forest_scene.
entries.limits: Static glTF trees from older exports (as in AlpineValley) still have no LOD chains; horizon-wide impostor grouping is still being verified.

entries.title: The Build panel in Studio
entries.summary: Building a game for a platform and estimating the size of its content now happens right in Studio, on the Publish tab.
body: The panel shows the game name, version and orientation, the platform list (macOS, iOS, Android, Web, Windows, Linux) with already built ones marked, and Release or Debug.

For the selected platform it shows which tools are present, which are missing and which Studio can install itself. "Estimate size" builds only the content pack and lists its size and heaviest files. The build log streams live; the finished build and the log open in Finder.
Studio never builds an unsaved project silently: it offers to save first.
entries.verified: On a Mac the tool table and size estimate were checked on a copy of the Lua Lab sample.
entries.limits: A full platform build from the panel has not been run yet. Branding and the asset audit are still in the old editor only.

entries.title: STRATA: Nanite-style cluster visualization
entries.summary: A debug view shows which clusters STRATA split the geometry into and which detail levels it selected in the frame: every cluster in its own colour.
body: StrataDebugView draws the selected cluster frontier over the frame — fill, wireframe or bounds — coloured by cluster, LOD depth, geometric error or material. Presentation only: LOD selection, routing and GPU data are unchanged, and the view is off by default.

The scene is procedural terrain (≈105 k triangles) and 20 rocks (≈82 k each), about 1.7 M source triangles in total. STRATA selected 15,280 clusters in the frame: small finest-level clusters up close, increasingly coarse ones towards the horizon.
entries.verified: Debug view in main (7d0654223). Frames captured with the tools/site/strata_showcase host (branch feature/site-strata-showcase, 4bf7232d4) on Linux, OpenGL through Mesa llvmpipe: 2 STRATA sources, 0 declined, 15,280 clusters, 1,384,090 debug triangles, 0 truncated, 1920×1080.
entries.limits: Not captured on Metal or other GPUs. Scene triangles are Morton-ordered: with the procedural mesh's original order clusters came out as strips — worth checking on real assets. STRATA rejects Sponza (cross-material seams).

entries.title: SpectraFX: campfires, a portal and fireflies in two scenes
entries.summary: Two scenes for the SpectraFX page: night in Sponza with campfires and a portal, and a sunset with clouds and volumetric fog. Five effects in the ordinary JSON format; particles light the scene.
body: The effects use the ordinary SpectraFX format and live in tools/site/fx_scene/fx. Campfire: a flame body, upright flame tongues, embers with trails, smoke and a warm light. Portal: two counter-rotating spark rings, a glowing rim, an inward swirl and a cold light. Plus rising motes at the portal, fireflies (some with small lights) and low mist.

The particle light module adds point lights to Renderer3D: 9 in the frame, lighting the arches, curtains and floor. PRISMA adds HDR, bloom, colour grading and a vignette; the sunset also uses the physical sky with clouds and god rays and volumetric fog (PRISMA local volumes).
entries.verified: Frames captured with the tools/site/fx_showcase.cpp host (branch feature/site-strata-showcase) on Linux, OpenGL through Mesa llvmpipe, 1920×1080. 6 s of simulation in 1/60 steps, then the frame is frozen. About 1,900 live particles, 9 particle lights. Recipe and commands: tools/site/fx_scene/README.md.
entries.limits: CPU particle backend only, no Metal GPU particles; not captured on Metal. Sponza is the Khronos glTF sample, not a game scene. Found while capturing: PRISMA draws the physical sky over particles seen against the sky, so they vanish — the sunset camera looks down. Trails of particles that only orbit render as vertical streaks.

entries.title: PRISMA: a camera at the water surface — waterline, film and drops
entries.summary: At the surface the frame splits along a waving waterline with a meniscus; after emerging, everything that was under water is covered by a refracting film that drains to the water level, leaving rivulets and drops.
body: lensWater tests the lens point of every pixel against NEREID's waving water plane: underwater optics below the line, the dry image above it, a bright refracting meniscus along it. Nothing runs down the part of the lens that is under water.

After emerging the film clings for the first third of sheetTime, then its ragged edge drains down, leaving meandering rivulets with a head drop and round lens drops with glints that dry over dryTime. Every parameter is tunable and the effect can be disabled.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: a real-time dive recording (a frame every ~0.35 s, video assembled at real speed); prisma_lens_water test.
entries.limits: The underside of the surface (total internal reflection) is not rendered separately yet; other backends are not visually verified.

entries.title: Depth of field: the blurred foreground is no longer cut out
entries.summary: Blurred foreground objects now spread over the background as in a real lens instead of ending on a hard line, as if cut out with scissors. The background still does not bleed onto a sharp foreground.
body: Before, blur at a depth boundary threw away everything on the other side: a near curtain or ivy kept a crisp outline over a blurred background, with ghosted patches next to it. Now every point of the frame gathers light from neighbours whose blur disc reaches it. Near blurred objects cover the background and the sharp zone, and what is behind them shows through their edge.

The rule respects sharpness: the background cannot bleed onto an object sharper than itself, so a sharp object in focus keeps a clean edge. The change is in PRISMA's metric depth of field, used by the LENS lens and the metricFocus setting.
entries.verified: A before/after pair was rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza with the same frame: a 35 mm f/1.4 lens focused at 4 m.
entries.limits: The new shader has not been compiled on OpenGL, WebGL or Vulkan yet. The pass is more expensive (32 samples per pixel instead of 8); its cost on weak mobile GPUs has not been measured.

entries.author: lens

entries.title: NEREID: water turbidity above and below the surface
entries.summary: Water gains a turbidity parameter (with a silt colour): one value changes both the look from above and the visibility when diving.
body: resolvedWaterOptics() turns turbidity into shared extinction, a milky silt colour and a scattering share; both the surface shader and PRISMA's underwater view read them. From above the water uses the real optical path — light down to the bed plus the slanted view ray — so turbid water also looks turbid from outside.
At 0 the water looks as before. The parameter lives in the surface style, the NereidWater component and cascades, is validated and is part of cache keys.
entries.verified: Mac (Metal), AlpineValley review copy: identical frames above and under water at 0 / 0.25 / 0.6; ecs_nereid_renderer_contract test.

entries.author: agent-wind-masks

entries.title: LENS: the lens sets exposure and depth of field
entries.summary: A camera can be described as a real lens — focal length, aperture, shutter, ISO and focus distance — and the frame gets its exposure and depth of field from them. Smooth camera rails for fly-throughs, camera shake and HDR frame recording to EXR were added.
body: Every camera in cameras.json now has a lens block. With driveExposure and driveDepthOfField on, the camera sets the frame brightness and the sharp zone itself: f/1.4 gives a short sharp zone and a strongly blurred background, f/8 keeps almost everything sharp. It is computed per camera, so the main view and the inset can use different lenses.

For fly-throughs the camera follows a rail through several points at an even speed, eases in and out, and the rail can loop. Shake is noise on six axes with a fade, identical on every run. The old linear rails and the previous shake behave as before.
Frames can be recorded as an OpenEXR sequence with the full HDR range, for editing, grading and render comparisons.
entries.verified: Rendered on a Mac (Metal) in Sponza at 1920×1080: a 35 mm f/1.4 lens focused at 4 m, with a second camera of the same scene in the inset. Exposure, depth of field, rails and EXR maths are covered by tests on Linux and Mac.
entries.limits: HDR recording to EXR is Metal-only for now; OpenGL records an 8-bit frame. Exposure is relative to a default lens, not in physical light units. Cubemaps, panoramas, mirrors, portals and stereo are not done yet.

media.caption: 35 mm f/1.4 lens focused at 4 m: the green curtain and column are sharp, the near blue curtain and the distance are blurred; the inset is a second camera

entries.author: lens

entries.title: Races in any project
entries.summary: A map with a "race" block turns its cars into a race: countdown, gates, laps, standings, bots on the track, a HUD and a chase camera.
body: A race is map data: checkpoint gates in driving order (the last one is the finish), a starting grid and a closed line for the bots. Rules set the countdown, the time to finish after the winner, a timeout and crash damage.

Gates count only in order, so shortcuts gain nothing. A car that is stuck, going the wrong way, wrecked or fallen off the world returns to its last gate. The race decides the match: the team in first place wins.

The same race, HUD and camera run on two kinds of maps: metre maps with colliders and grid maps with heroes. Controls, car physics and spline roads are shared. There are two sample games: the Oval Sprint oval and the Road Circuit along a spline road with trucks whose wheels roll and steer.
entries.verified: Bots complete three laps on both samples; a save in the middle of a race continues exactly as without it; other metre-map games play as before.
entries.limits: Getting in and the look of the cars still differ between the two map kinds: on metre maps cars are drawn as boxes.

entries.title: Client builds take only the engine modules they need
entries.summary: game.json can choose which optional engine parts go into the packaged game, or leave it to detection: "engineModules": ["auto"].
body: Every packaged game used to carry the whole engine: particles, Spine, gamepads, FBX and legacy model loaders, the city server client, traffic and map generation. Now a packaging.engineModules list, shared or per platform, can leave them out.

"auto" looks into the project: Spine and gamepad from game.json, particles from effect files, loaders from source models, simulations from rules and maps. If the game uses something excluded, the packager refuses with a clear error; without the field everything builds as before.

On a test macOS client build the executable shrank by about 7% just from linking only the code in use. Each disabled module removes from about a hundred kilobytes (gamepad) to a couple of megabytes (particles, legacy model loaders).
entries.verified: The packager checks the module choice for Web, Windows and macOS; sizes were measured on the macOS client.
entries.limits: HTML5 build size and startup are not measured yet: Emscripten was missing on the build machine. Android, iOS, Windows and Linux have not been built with modules off either.

entries.title: LENS: cameras as scene data, a Studio window and agent tools
entries.summary: A game's cameras are now described in one cameras.json file: several cameras, their draw order, their own render targets and frame capture. They can be created and edited in a Studio window or through the agent's MCP tools.
body: Each camera is a scene entity with its own components: transform, lens, follow rig, render target. The engine orders the cameras itself when one shows the image of another and warns about cycles.
Secondary cameras — monitors, picture-in-picture, portraits — get the same prepared frame as the main view: the game is not simulated again and animation does not step twice.

Studio has a cameras window: list, create, save and reload. Agents do the same through MCP: lens_scene_get, lens_camera_set and the related operations validate a change before writing and leave the working file intact on error. Any camera's frame can be saved to PNG.
entries.verified: The cameras window was opened in Studio on a Mac with a project and its camera loaded; the client with cameras enabled rendered the game scene on Metal. Replaying the frame into a secondary camera was compared pixel by pixel with the main frame on Metal.
entries.limits: The pixel comparison has only been run on Metal; Vulkan and mobile GPUs are not checked yet. Cost with many cameras has not been measured.

entries.title: GI probes: moment-based visibility instead of a plane
entries.summary: Probe visibility is stored as Chebyshev moments — the dark band on the Sponza arches is gone.
body: A rebake replaces only the 96 visibility texels per probe; sun, sky and point-light transport stay the same. Sponza — 10,710 probes and 10.8 M triangles — rebakes in about 18 seconds on two cores.
An old plane-visibility cache renders bit-identically to before the change (maximum channel difference 0).
entries.verified: Cloud Linux, llvmpipe GLES 3.2: High before/after captures, HDR GPU checks 1–53 pass on Linux GL.
entries.limits: Moments still leak slightly through thin geometry; probes inside geometry are not relocated. MSL, Metal captures and Android are unverified.

entries.title: Light baking: lightmaps and probes
entries.summary: The engine's own offline CPU path tracer writes lightmaps for static objects and terrain and a probe grid for everything that moves.
body: Map lights are marked mixed (stay realtime, their bounce is baked) or baked (lightmap and probes only). The runtime blends baked light with the realtime sun, like mixed lighting in Unity.

Rebakes are skipped when nothing changed: the bake stores a 64-bit hash of geometry, materials, textures, transforms, lights and settings. Available in the editor (Graphics → Light baking) and through MCP: lightbake_set, lightbake_bake, lightbake_status.
